utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Lukic, you go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just want to direct Your Honours' attention to the filing from yesterday by the Defence. It's our request for non-sitting week for Easter period, meaning Orthodox Easter. So, we are facing the same problems as we did during the January holidays, so we -- we -- it's almost impossible for us. People do not want to talk to us at all. They should be here and be prepared during Easter, if they want to, and Easter Sunday, if we want to lead them. So we would kindly ask you to consider our problems and we explained that everything is going smoothly and we do not want any -- any interruptions and we would have some probably, many, during that week, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand for Orthodox Christmas, I think, we tried to accommodate you, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still have to consider whether we do the same for Orthodox Easter. To be fair to you, we had already a non-sitting week on our minds. I'm not going to tell you which one, but it was not the one you have on our mind and we had some other reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not object to that non-sitting week either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's in everyone's interest to proceed. Not only in the interests of the international community and the Chamber but also in the interests of the accused. We'll certainly pay proper attention to your filing, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're doing the mathematics today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm reluctant to try my hand at mathematics in the morning, Your Honour. But I did want to address the issue that arose yesterday with MFI P7167. I've checked our records and the situation is we have two versions of the document in the original B/C/S, 1st Krajina Corps document number 485. One of those versions, the version uploaded in this case we got from the 1st Krajina Corps collection, it includes eight names. One of those versions we got from a Defence team in a previous trial. That includes nine names in both English and the B/C/S. I provided it to Mr. Lukic this morning. And we agreed that under the circumstances, the most practical thing would be that we would simply rely on the names that are in the 1st Krajina Corps collection version and not address the matter -- or not clarify the matter further. We've reviewed the document, the remainder of the B/C/S text is identical in the two versions. There is a addition, an ordinal number in the top right-hand corner. You can see in the English, it is 131/3. The B/C/S of the version we received from that previous Defence team which has an ERN number one number earlier has the ordinal number is 130/3 so my impression is that relates to that previous trial but we won't be relying on or seeking to ascribe meaning to those four digits either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and just for the transcript, I think you said the one you received from the Defence tame was 130-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. In line 7 of temporary transcript page 3, I'm correctly recorded to have said 131/3 and I see line 9 has now correctly recorded me 130/3 [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it is now corrected. Yes, of course, it's always a bit worrying to know that there are two identical -- to -- two different versions of one and the same document, but if the parties agree that in itself with eight or nine names that such an order was issued, then I don't think that the Chamber will insist on further exploring the -- the cause of the variation. Then the English version was with the -- at this moment the translation was the one with the eight names or the nine names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Nine names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nine names. So we now need an English version to be uploaded with only the nine names -- the eight names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mathematics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm relieved to see that I'm not the only one who struggles with them in the morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm a bit surprised by myself that even under ten I have difficulties in doing the math correctly. Above ten, I was used to that, but ... Let's leave it to that. Once the correct version has been uploaded, if it has been done, it should be attached --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll inform the Chamber once that's been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then if that's all done, the witness can be escorted in the courtroom. And I use the opportunity to deal with a small matter. It is a remaining issue from the testimony of Cedo Sipovac. On the 12th of November of last year, during the testimony of Cedo Sipovac, D767, D768, and D769 were marked for identification. On 3rd of February of this year, Defence submitted that it considered the admission of these documents through another witness instead of tendering them through Sipovac. After the Prosecution had objected to the letter, the Defence indicated it would advise the Chamber at a later date whether it would argue the Prosecution's objections or whether it would seek to tender the document through another witness. On 24th of February the Defence was unable to advise the Chamber of its position on this. The Chamber then expected the Defence to respond later that same week, and this can be found at transcript page 32206. As at today's date, the Defence has not responded, and the Chamber wonders whether it could receive the position of the Defence relating to the documents D767, D768, and D769. Mr. Lukic, it's not a long story I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. Now we are certain that the witness who issued those documents will testify in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore you leave them as they are, and you'll tender them through that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krcmar. Apologies for continuing to deal with administrative matters when you entered the courtroom, but we'll now continue. Mr. Traldi will continue his cross-examination, and I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 32105 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as it is, good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is the rules and regulations for the work of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war in the zone of responsibility of the East Bosnia Corps. I just want to look at one point quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 5 in the B/C/S and 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the top of the page in the B/C/S and towards the bottom in the English we see point 13, and it says that: "The exchange of prisoners of war shall be conducted on the one-for-one basis (soldier for soldier, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person), or on the all-for-all basis." Is it right that the category of prisoners of war exchanged by the corps commissions also included women and elderly persons, as well as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- these are regulations of the IBK -- corps, not my corps. I did not have such rules. In principle, all exchanges should have been all for all. If no such agreement could be arrived then it would be one for one, but according to our rules, we did not exchange a woman for a woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krcmar, the question still stands: Were there women and elderly people amongst your prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area where I worked, that did not exist. In the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, we did not have any imprisoned women. There was just one case, a woman who was charged with spying, and she was exchanged for another prisoner of war. These are the regulations of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, not of the 1st Krajina Corps, whose member I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm putting to you is that soldiers is a distinct category, and there are also other categories because the VRS corps exchange commissions also exchanged people who were not soldiers, not properly prisoners of war. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that prisoners of war were exchanged for other prisoners of war. People who were in military prisons, those run by the corps, not civilian wards and again I'm speaking on behalf of the 1st Krajina Corps. I remind you that I worked in the 1st Krajina Corps, not in the East Bosnia Corps, and I cannot testify on behalf of the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, unless you know something about it. Witness, again -- Mr. Traldi perhaps you should split up your questions always: Did this happen in the corps for which this witness was responsible or does he have any knowledge about it happening in any other corps. Because you are constantly asking your questions in the plural, corps, with an S and commissions, with an S, whereas, the witness always says, I can't testify about that. And let me be very clear, Witness, if you know something, you should tell us, irrespective or whether it was from your commission or any -- or from a commission of any other corps of the VRS. Let that be clear to you. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 32105 receives number P7169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can we have P4008.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an order you also saw during direct examination, from General Tolimir issued the 3rd of October, 1994. As a first question, we see the Muslims are going to receive prisoners from the Foca prison, Rudo prison, Visegrad prison, and parts of prisoners from Batkovic and Butmir. None of those prisons were in the 1st Krajina Corps' area of responsibility were they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, how is it that you were able to express a view on the exchange policy expressed in this document when otherwise you have been unable to express a view on exchanges conducted by the commissions of other corps?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says in paragraph, the last one or the penultimate one, that Dragan Bulajic will be in charge of the exchange. That's why I think that the exchange was organised by the civilian commission, i.e., Dragan Bulajic. It doesn't seem that any of the corps was involved in the negotiations about this particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see here in the third paragraph that General Tolimir is writing that the Main Staff has sent the text of the draft agreement on prisoner exchange and lists of prisoners to the area of responsibility of, as he puts it, "your corps." And we see at the top that it's addressed to the SRK, the IBK, the Herzegovina Corps and the Drina Corps. Below that, we read that: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps will not receive the lists considering that they have a member in the state commission for exchange and that he is in possession of the full documentation." Do you know who the SRK's member in the state commission for exchange was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday at transcript page 32469 that General Tolimir was one of the Main Staff officers who would issue approval for exchanges. You don't have any personal knowledge as to how he was involved - or not - in negotiating this particular exchange, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he participated in the negotiations for this particular exchange. However, the Main Staff issued instructions and approvals for our exchanges when we turned to them. Whether there was somebody in the state commission or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence - P6722 for the parties - that in the ensuing exchange, the Bosnian Serbs freed 247 prisoners, which included 19 Bosnian army soldiers, as well as numbers of women, children, elderly people, and people who were physically challenged. Were you aware of how this exchange or how the exchange that arose from this order was eventually conducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that he cannot answer without the document. Even I don't remember anymore what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think if I was asking him to express details about the exchange or comment on the document, I could see that. All I was asking the witness was whether he was aware of those facts, yes or no, and I'm happy to call it up, but I think it's straightforward enough for him to tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. You asked the witness whether he has any recollection of what you just mentioned, and if he has not, it may refresh his recollection if he would have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It may or it may not be necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands. The witness is not asked to tell us anything about the document but it's just for reference and for the Chamber and the Defence that you refer to this document. Now, Witness, Mr. Traldi will put the question to you again. Carefully listen to it and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'll try to frame it very precisely, sir, the Chamber has received evidence that there was an exchange conducted pursuant to the same agreement we see reflected here and that in that exchange, the Bosnian Serbs freed 247 prisoners, those prisoners included 19 Bosnian army soldiers, as well as numbers of women, children, elderly people, and people who were physically challenged. Were you aware of the facts that I've just recited.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, because the 1st Krajina Corps where I worked was not involved in this exchange. Had it been involved I would have probably known. But, no, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, just tell us you don't know. You don't have to explain why you do not know something. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I'm going to turn to one matter that you discuss in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 00872.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from the VRS Main Staff dated the 8th of June, 1993. It refers to the exchange of prisoners of war and it refers in the first paragraph to a massive exodus of Serbs and Croats across HVO-controlled territories to the territory of Republika Srpska. In the second paragraph, we see what appears to be an instruction that this exodus should "be used to force the Croatian side to unconditionally release all prisoners of war from the VRS, VRSK, and the former JNA and all civilians who wish to leave the Croatian-controlled parts of the former BH." Now, you describe this incident as a rescue of Croats in your statement. Your commission and the 1st Krajina Corps received instructions to use that exodus to force the Croatian side to facilitate an exchange of Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd put to you we see that policy clearly reflected in this document. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I put to you is that I took part in the freeing of the Croatian population in Central Bosnia and their transfer across the border. They were in conflict with the Muslim army and there were no conditions that were set forth. I personally took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, we see this is dated 8th of June. The Chamber has received evidence that a POW camp at Manjaca was set up and several hundred Croats held there on the 8th of June -- on or about the 8th of June, 1993. Is it your evidence that you weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that for me? I'm afraid that I have misunderstood. I do not see the date on the document. Could you please help me with that at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the top left corner, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see 1993, but I don't see the month. I don't see the date as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand it's not terribly clear on the screen, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a euphemism, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I certainly hadn't intended it that way, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and let's see whether the date as it appears in the English version finds its -- a proper basis in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Often the scanned version doesn't fully reflect what the interpreters are able to work with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we should have a look at the version on the basis of which the 8th of June is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go to the next page in B/C/S. Sometimes a date appears there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we look at the end, there will be a stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wherein which the 10th of June appears as the date on which this document was processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So is it clear to you now, sir, that we're talking at least about the month of June in the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen here now. The 10th of June, 1993. That's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what I was putting to you was that on or about the 8th of June, 1993, the Chamber has received evidence that a POW camp at Manjaca was set up to hold Croats from Vares. Is it your evidence that you weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The POW camp at Manjaca? That is not the purpose for which it was established. If you allow me to explain, Your Honours? Yes. There was an unknown number of Croat people from Central Bosnia that we took over and, quite simply, we transported them through Republika Srpska towards Croatia and third countries. Also, a large number of wounded persons. I personally took them over. They were in Banja Luka for 15 days, as far as I know, until conditions were created for their departure. All of them were members of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, so this is certainly not a question of prisoners and POW camps. All of this was done for humane reasons. At the time, my duty and obligation was towards the wounded of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, our problem is that the document says otherwise. Are you aware of that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what the document says. But I'm speaking from my own practice, what happened on the ground and how this was actually being done, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 2 in the English as well. In, sorry, in both languages. I hadn't realised we'd moved back in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At point 7, we read that: "Reports on all exchanges are to be regularly submitted to the Main Staff. Upon the completion of the all-for-all exchange process, when we make sure that all our prisoners have been exchanged, we shall release the Zarko Tole group and the Croatian extremists from HVO units who surrendered." So I have two questions for you about this language. First, we see, again, a reference to a planned exchange of these persons; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are persons who were prisoners of war, like Zarko Tole, an officer of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while most of these prisoners had been taken recently as a result of that surrender, Mr. Tole had, in fact, been in VRS custody for more than a year at this point and had been transferred through the VRS camp system; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zarko Tole is a classical POW. And he has nothing to do with this release of people from Central Bosnia. Zarko Tole was in the official prisons of Republika Srpska, not in camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... wondering whether you are talking at cross-purposes. What Mr. Traldi puts to you is that in paragraph 7 he reads that, first, there will be an exchange. And once that's totally completed, that then Zarko Tole group and the Croatian extremists who had surrendered are to be released. So we have two matters, and I think the question of Mr. Traldi was about the first issue, that is, the exchange of prisoners, first, to be completed; and then the second issue is who should, after that, be released. Now, Mr. Traldi asked you whether this paragraph indeed confirms that there was an exchange of prisoners planned, whereas your answer was about the second part, that is, what should happen after that exchange of prisoners has been completed. So - Mr. Traldi, if I understood your question well about the exchange of prisoners, could you first answer the question whether this, again, confirms that an exchange of prisoners was planned and leave out, for the time being, the Zarko Tole group and what should happen after that. Could you answer that first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's easier for me this way. An exchange of POWs had just been planned that had been agreed on earlier. It was planned as stated in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think that answers the question by Mr. Traldi. He asked whether the document expresses that an exchange of prisoners was planned, and you say, yes, that's what happened. Therefore the next question perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The second question I asked was just Mr. Tole he had been in VRS custody and I'm not contesting that he was a classical prisoner of war. He been in VRS custody for more than a year. At that point had been transferred from Manjaca to Batkovic within the system of detention facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle I did not in which prison Zarko Tole was. I did negotiate his exchange but once the exchange an agreed upon then I address the security department and I ask for a POW to be made available for exchanges. All the POWs that I took over were taken over only for -- from military prisons, the three military prisons that were within the area of responsibility of the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document number 00872 receives number P7170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7170 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one quick question. Was Mr. Tole detained in VRS custody for more than a year at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32099.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, this will be the last document I show you. As it comes up, during direct examination you talked about some graves in the Sarajevo area. Now, you became aware of the information you've provided about Sarajevo after the war in the course of your work; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified at transcript page 32412 that 471 Serbs have been exhumed in Sarajevo. The Sarajevo area, as I understand, makes up ten municipalities. Does the figure of 471 Serbs include exhumations wherever in that ten municipality area they may have been conducted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just municipalities that were under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned specifically the grave in the Lav cemetery. Are you aware - yes or no - that forensic analysis has revealed some of the bodies exhumed from the Lav cemetery over the years died of wounds from shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The post-mortem findings would show that if we had them here. I've already said it was a violent death. We cannot talk about that without the post-mortem findings, and that is the field of forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, I wasn't asking you to offer a medical opinion. I was simply asking whether you were aware - yes or no - that post-mortem findings had reached that conclusion. Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered. And just one more thing in relation to this grave, if the Chamber -- oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you have not answered that question. Second, the question is not whether rightly or wrongly these conclusions were made. The question is whether in these autopsy reports it is stated that people died from shelling wounds or sniping wounds. Right or wrong, but whether you have read what is at the bottom of such a report and whether it says or whether it says tuberculosis, or whether it says sniping wound, that is the simple question that is put to you, whether such findings, whether you read them when you looked at the reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read these reports, and I have the English version here of whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English version of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As -- just -- you have not read the outcome of the autopsy reports, the post-mortems? You have no idea about what they say as to the cause of death of some of the people that were exhumed in the Lav grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read most of it, but I have 4100 post-mortem reports and it's hard for me to say anything now. That's why I said we need to have the autopsy report here and now, because I cannot speak just off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand you don't recall today whether you may have at one point have known that some of the people exhumed from Lav over the years may have been killed by shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, because you've just said "maybe." And I'm saying "maybe" too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Witness, I asked you whether you had ever seen such conclusions at the end of post-mortem autopsy reports. Your answer was: I haven't read these reports. Now, one minute later, your answer is: I don't remember what the content was of what I read. The one is not the same as the other. Would you agree with that or do you have any explanation as why you said that you hadn't read them and a minute later you say you don't remember because there were too many you have read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain because you confused me here with this English document that I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I told you that this document has nothing do with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rather, listen carefully then. But we now do understand that you have read the reports and that you do not exclude for the possibility that at least some of the person exhumed in the grave were reported as having died from shelling or sniping consequences. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a report of the United Nations commission of experts from 1994. Looking at page -- at paragraph 13, the commission is reporting that: "Since the beginning of the siege it is estimated that nearly 10.000 persons have been killed or are missing in the city. This total includes over 1.500 children." Now have you become aware in the course of your work of reports that, in the first two years of the siege of Sarajevo, nearly 10.000 persons were killed or went missing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard quite a lot of information, but I see I know now that this information was incorrect. If you allow me, I have testified, and in my report, I even stated that the minister of foreign affairs said at the UN that 250.000 people were killed, Bosniak, in 1992. And we see today that that was not true. This is questionable as well. To this day, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we don't know. Records of missing persons have not been set up. And over here, we have some figures that, quite simply, cannot be considered reliable data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, "My report," what are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand. Which report of mine do you mean. Or it's a mistranslation. Poor interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "If you allow me, I have testified, and in my report, I even stated that the minister of foreign affairs said at the UN that," et cetera. Which report are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not report. Statement. In my statement. That's it. And I still haven't got my statement here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you -- if you ask for it, then it will be provided to you. It's no problem. So you were referring to your statement rather than to a report. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a long document. I'd ask that it be marked for identification. We'll speak with the Defence about making a selection. And I won't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document 32099 receives number P7171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7171 is marked for identification. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'd need P7160 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my colleague Mr. Traldi put questions to you about this; namely, whether you knew that the chief of the Security Services Centre gave this statement on the 28th of April, 1992. Do you remember today where you were on the 28th of April, 1992? In which formation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I don't know. At that point in time, military units, civilian police units, there was that transfer, I'm not sure of the date. It was more than 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, there's a reference to SOS, members of SOS. However, the speech itself, is it in the present tense or is it the future tense? Is something that is already happened being referred to, or something that is yet to happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what paragraph you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. The third paragraph in the text, in bold. "Soon special detachments," and so on and so forth. Could you see whether this is something that is yet to be organised or that it already has been organised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this, it means that they will -- yes, they will deal with renegades, they shall deal with renegades from different formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to be confused by this document, so we don't need it on our screens any longer. Yesterday, a video was shown to you and a man is being treated rather harshly, a man wearing civilian clothing in a garage. On the basis of this video recording, could you conclude whether this was a Serb, a Croat or a Muslim, I mean, this man who was wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The video could not show it -- I mean, one could not conclude on the basis of the video who was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw Nenad Stevandic's insignia on his pocket. Do you remember after all this time whether these markings were repeated after a while and how often they would be valid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be valid for two or three days, depending on the assessment of the command, how long it should be worn. Sometimes it would be one day; sometimes it would be five days. I don't know. I cannot remember. I mean, I don't want to say I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P3711, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, on page 32428 of our transcript, lines 15 through 19, you say that the judges who had come from Zenica, the prosecutor, who had come from Zenica were telling you about the unit of Burce, or from Burce. It's clear to you, but for the record, you need to tell us where -- where in Bosnia and Herzegovina Zenica is, and what the ethnicity of this judge and this prosecutor is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica is in the Federation. The judge who was there from Zenica was Mr. Hilmo Ahmetovic. The prosecutor was Redzo Delic. The police was the police from Zenica. At that moment, I acted as host or monitor. I followed their work, and it is only natural that we discussed the case, that is to say, this crime. And they presented what they knew, and I said yesterday what it was that I heard from them. That was sometime in 1998. 1998, I think it's 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have difficulties in finding it on the page reference you gave, that is 32428.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 458.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Lines 15 to 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question again. You are clear, but for the record, what were the ethnicities of the judges, the prosecutor, and the police who arrived from Zenica who told you about the Burce units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the judge or the prosecutor from Zenica tell you how they had obtained that information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything about that. They only told me that they had information about that and that it was the Burce group who this had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have probably ten more minutes and then I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, I take it that if this information was given to the witness, it must be recorded somewhere which would certainly strengthen very much the testimony of the witness. It would corroborate -- so if there's any documentation available, then, of course, the Chamber would very much appreciate if it would be there, so that we can -- because it's -- on the basis of the testimony of yesterday that there are at least on an exhumation to tell someone immediately after that who was the perpetrator, of course, is not what usually happens but if there is documentation confirming that, then we'd certainly like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We -- we tried to find yesterday, Your Honours, and we did find -- we did find some mentioning of Chetniks from Burce doing some crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you mean not in the exhumation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think it should and it would be in the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is any interview with witnesses who may have been at the exhumation site. I don't know how it was reported and that's exactly what I'm saying, that if there's any report of that exhumation which would give support to the -- to the testimony of the witness, which at least there are still a few questions to be raised on the basis of what the witness could tell us, then we would appreciate to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll probably have to look into the records of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For example. Or ask the assistance of the Prosecution. Or seek a request from the authorities so that we would not just have the testimony but it would be corroborated by documentary evidence. Or any follow-up evidence. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, there was a request that you address the matter of the shifting of the burden of proof. Could you give us an indication as to how much time would you need for that, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One minute, on my part, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krcmar, we will come to an end really soon. Let me ask you something about the topic that Judge Orie raised. Did you perhaps note the information that you had received from the judge and the prosecutor from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We co-operated on a daily basis on exhumations. We discussed many issues, including that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the results of the investigation that was carried out by the Zenica District Court?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would the judges inform you about the results of any investigations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We received feedback only within the area of exhumations. When it came to investigations, that was not part of our job, and we did not receive information about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P7165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to fully understand your previous answer. Are you saying that your knowledge was limited to what you exchanged during the exhumations; and whether there was an investigation as a follow-up, you wouldn't know anything about that. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about this document. My attention was drawn by the fact that the document was signed by Colonel Gojko Vujnovic, the desk officer for co-operation with UNPROFOR and civilian affairs. My question is this: Did UNPROFOR or any other international organisation such as the Red Cross take part in the exchanges at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, especially the International Red Cross. UNPROFOR was also in presence or -- at all those exchanges or the transfer of people from one side to the other because people did not leave prisons to go directly from a prison to be exchanged. They would come from their homes to cross over to the other territory and then proceed to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P7170.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already seen this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that. You are aware that you, again, yourself used the word "exchange"? "... did not leave prisons to go directly from a prison to be exchanged." So you are talking about exchanges, as was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just a terminology issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to that. You said that people did not go directly from prisons to be exchanged when you spoke about exchanges, i.e., about transfers. Did you have in mind people who were in prison or those who were at home?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were at home. So we cannot use the term "exchange." It was a simple transfer from one territory to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What we have before us is P7170, and we can see that this is a document which was issued by the Main Staff. It was received on the 10th of June, 1993. The typed name is that of Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. It says that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to read more slowly. Could you resume where the transcript says: "It says that ..." And then start your quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "The exodus to the Croats to the territory of Republika Srpska and the surrender of HVO units to VRS units should be used to force the Croatian side to unconditionally release all prisoners of war from the VRS, VRSK, and the former JNA and all civilians to wish to leave the Croatian-controlled parts of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina." First of all, do you know whether in 1993 there was still members of the JNA in Croatian prisons.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission of Yugoslavia was looking for prisoners of war from the JNA from Croatia. The lot of some of those people is still not nope. We only knew or, rather, it was well-known that members of the JNA were being held in Croatian prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we have seen, the document was issued on the 8th of June or around that date. And now look -- let's look at P3683. I would like to jog your memory by saying that the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that Croats left Travnik on the 6th of June, 1993. Here, we see a document that was issued on the 7th of June, 1993. This document was also signed by Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. Under 1, the title of the document is: Treatment of HVO members and of the Croatian civilian population. It was sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. "With regard the situation that has been created in the sector of Travnik, act in accordance with my verbal order which has to do with the following ..." Under 1, it says: "The civilian population and persons not fit for combat should be transferred to the sector of Novska in Croatian territory. "An adequate number of motor vehicles should be engaged, and this is to be done through the International Committee of the Red Cross." Did you comply with this order, i.e., with item 1?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We did exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 2, it says: "For intelligence purposes question persons fit for military service and HVO units' members (of the Frankopan Brigade) and then until further notice accommodate them at Manjaca." Do you know if that -- this was complied with and who did it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was within the purview of the military intelligence and security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the civilians who were transferred to the territory of Croatia, had there been any requests made in respect of them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no conditions set. They were transferred from the territory of Republika Srpska. They were accompanied by the International Committee of the Red Cross, and they were handed over to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many days were needed to do that? Did they spend a night anywhere, or did they continue travelling to Croatia? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that provisions were secured for those people. I went there to take over prisoners of war. My other colleagues accompanied those people. I believe that the journey lasted a couple of days, but I'm not sure. Prisoners of war or, rather, the wounded spent over ten days in the hospital in Banja Luka and then I handed them over to the Croatian side without any conditions having been set. They just crossed over to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question. It also says that people should be accommodated in Manjaca. Were they free to leave Manjaca as they wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that the HVO unit would be accommodated at Manjaca and that interviews would be conducted with them. Later, they were all unconditionally set free. Not for a single moment they were subject of any negotiations or conversations regarding an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind if you want to read it as you wish to read it. But that's not what the document says. The document says: "... persons fit for military service and HVO units' members ..." The document is also about the civilian population. So if I ask you whether people were free to leave Manjaca, yes or no, first of all, what you are telling me is not an answer to my question. Second, it misreads the document. If you want to do that, fine. But you should be aware that it does remain unnoticed. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know of any civilians which were detained at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no civilians, as far as I know. They were accompanied in a different way, and they went in the direction of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's a reference to two categories here under item 2: Those who were fit for service; and members of the Frankopan Brigade of the HVO. Do you know when an agreement was reached for all the militarily able-bodied and members of the Frankopan Brigade of the HVO to be accommodated at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 6 - we need the following page in English, please - it says: "Within the limits of your capabilities, provide care for the civilian population until they are evacuated to the territory of Croatia. Conduct yourselves correctly toward the HVO members and able-bodied people until their status has been resolved." Do you know how the status of those people who were accommodated at Manjaca was resolved?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. They went to Croatia. There were no negotiations about any exchange, there were no conditions set, but they left after the civilians. And they did not have the status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, it's not clear to me, you said: "Those who were accommodated in Manjaca, they left after the civilians ..." But I do understand that at least part of those accommodated in Manjaca were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the document, "able-bodied men." Those were members of the HVO, as far as I know. I don't know that they were civilians. They were HVO members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what the document says. I'm quite happy that you interpret it in that way. But both in the paragraph that we looked at and also in paragraph 4 of this document, it clearly distinguishes between able-bodied persons and members of HVO units. Therefore, I assume if you just call them -- if the document is about civilian population, if you say the able-bodied persons should be sent to Manjaca together with the HVO member units, first, that these are two different categories; and, second, if someone is a soldier, I would not call him an able-bodied person, I would call him a soldier. I understand, but please correct me when my understanding is wrong, an able-bodied person, someone who is physically fit to be a soldier but not a soldier yet. Have you any comment on this understanding of this terminology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Able-bodied men can be civilians, and all civilians left the territory of Republika Srpska and went to Croatia within the next two days. Members of the HVO were kept behind them, but they left thereafter. I'm not aware of the fact that civilians were ever sent to Manjaca. I and all of my colleagues were directly involved in that operation with a view to helping those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have paragraph 8 - we need the next page in both versions - we see number 8. It says that: "... the ill and wounded should be taken care of in our medical institutions." You've already testified about that, haven't you, that you took part in that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was precisely in charge of that, that is to say of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to look at P7171 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this - the document is in English - you were asked about the Lav graveyard, whether you knew how people were wounded, and you said, I cannot manage without autopsy reports. My question: Was it easier for you to get to the mortal remains of these 36 Serbs and three Muslims that were buried underneath the corpses of newborn babies and other corpses? How did you get to that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, we could not reach any kind of agreement with the federal commission. That is why the intervention of the high representative was required and we had to provide lots and lots of relevant evidence to persuade the Office of the High Representative and the IPTF that indeed there was a grave there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The federal authorities, did they deny the existence of a grave there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And they even carried out objections with some of the family members who had family members buried there and their newborn children. They were saying that we were violating their graves and underneath, indeed, there was this other grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krcmar. That is all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly, Mr. President. Could we have, first, P7095. Further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, we see here a document from the HVO, from the military intelligence service, dated the 19th of June, 1993. In the second paragraph, we read that: "At the negotiations in Celebic, representatives of the Serb side offers 1789 civilians from the Lasva area for exchange, 500 of them children, 471 men eligible for military service, which the Serbs deem to be HVO soldiers and 29 wounded HVO members who are located in hospital in Banja Luka. In return, they are seeking that all civilians of Serb ethnicity from Rascani (outside Tomislavgrad) and Livno municipality, and others ... be released."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now if we could have P7096.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that: "In accordance with the talks held in Geneva on the 24th of June, 1993, between the presidents of the RH and the Republic of Serbia, as well as the highest representatives of the Croatian and Serbian people in BiH, Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Radovan Karadzic, particularly with regard to the agreement on exchange of detainees and release of civilians is hereby ordered to civilian military and police authorities of Livno and Tomislavgrad to ensure an unobstructed departure of all members of Serbian people from the areas of these municipalities (this pertains to those who wish to do so) to the territory under Serb control." Now, you testified a moment ago that the Serb -- or, rather, the Croat civilians transferred out of Central Bosnia in June 1993 were not exchanged. Were you unaware of the large-scale exchange reflected in these documents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there is a mistake in terms of terminology here. As we can see from this document from Geneva, this meant unhindered crossing over of the Serb population and then there was this other document that we saw, instructions from General Mladic to help the civilian population cross over. There was no exchange. It's just a question of terminology. Whether it is crossing over, or whether it is an exchange. So it's just the wrong terminology that is being used here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if the two sides agree, we'll let your civilians cross over but only if you only let our civilians cross over, in your view, that's not an exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are no civilians of ours. This means rescuing the Croatian people from Central Bosnia, from the Lasva river valley. They were in a conflict with the Muslims. We were saving these people. Please do not reduce this humanitarian endeavour to a mere exchange. This was a major humanitarian effort, a humane thing to do, and I personally took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 08203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, could I put one very short, simple question, Witness. We talked a lot about Manjaca and HVO members' unit and able-bodied men to be accommodated there. Were you there? Have you visited Manjaca in that specific time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we have now 65 ter 08203.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this in regard to your evidence that international organisations participated in exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last paragraph on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We read: "Both sides are 'releasing' civilians to the other side, as well as exchanging groups of civilians, very often without making available any information to UNHCR, ICRC or UNPROFOR. This is thinly disguised ethnic cleansing but mostly very difficult to detect." Now we see -- if we go back to the first page, that this is a document coming from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the rest of the paragraph has to be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to read the full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Traldi will do so. He is following your suggestion. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could have page 2 back on the screen. The final paragraph reads: "Both sides are releasing civilians to the other side, as well as exchanging groups of civilian, very often without making available any information to UNHCR, ICRC or UNPROFOR. This is thinly disguised ethnic cleansing but mostly very difficult to detect. At the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo Bridge in Sarajevo, groups of civilians are regularly exchanged between the sides, but within the agreed times of freedom of movement, when it is not possible to separate civilians being exchanged from those with permission to visit the city or Grbavica." Now my question, in regard to the evidence that you gave on re-direct was simply: Were you aware that UNPROFOR had expressed concerns that the exchange of civilians was thinly disguised ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text that you read out speaks of crossing over from one side to the other. From the text, we do not see that people are coming from prisons and that exchange is being carried out. I did not know about this, what UNPROFOR said, but I want to say that this has to do with -- with crossing over as you read it out, not exchanges. Again I repeat, it's a question of terminology. What is crossing over? What is a release? What is an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, it uses the word "exchanges" at least twice, I think three times in the paragraph I read to you. I'd put to you you're reluctant to use the term itself because you are aware of precisely this sort of allegation that the exchange of civilians was part of the machinery of ethnic cleansing. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are putting this wrongly and you are putting it into the context of people who did highly honourable work, released people who were POWs and you are projecting this as some kind of ethnic cleansing machinery. I didn't know what was happening in Sarajevo. I lived in Banja Luka. I worked in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps. However, what you are doing is not right and not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose we should have it translated so I'd ask that be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 08203 receives number P7172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, exceptionally, I would just ask this witness to take off his headphones since he does not speak any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the witness understand the English language? I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I would kindly ask Your Honour, or Your Honours, to ask this witness if he knows whether the last two documents shown to him, actually two -- last P documents have anything to do with the operation of a transporting Croat civilians from mid-Bosnia to Croatia since it is obvious that it just has to be established whether since 6th of June until 19th of June anybody from this group was still in Bosnia-Herzegovina for these 13 days. Our claim is that these two documents have nothing to do with the operation this witness was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I immediately noticed when I looked at this document because we are seriously looking at any document that this is a document dated 20 July 1994 and I therefore, in this context, did not understand Mr. Traldi to specifically address what happened in early June 1993 but that he put a rather broader question to the witness and so -- so, therefore, there should be no confusion that a document, of course, in July 1994 is -- is not expressing or not -- not specifically addressing a matter which happened in June 1993 would be only very indirectly related to events going on and not specifically. That's, at least, how I looked at it, but I'm looking at my colleagues whether they have any different views, but you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P7095 is from 9th June and 7096 is from 25th June. Does that, according to the Prosecution, has the same meaning where they presented those documents or they want to claim that those two documents actually show what happened in regard of the action Mr. Krcmar took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I had intended to suggest that P7095 and 7096 related to the exchanges. I hadn't intended to suggest that the July 1994 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I would kindly ask Your Honours to ask this witness whether before 19 June, the transport of both civilians and military men was finished and according to our witness, Kolenda Davor, everything was finished long time ago, long before this date. According to him, they were transported on the 12th and 13th of June, military men to -- and before that, all the civilians has -- have already left Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if the Prosecution wants to claim this had any to do with the group Mr. Krcmar took place in transporting, then we think that it's misleading of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's try to keep it also procedurally on the right track. Of course, you said exceptionally, Mr. Lukic, because it's not common that after the -- after the further cross-examination by the Prosecution that the Defence has an other opportunity to examine the witness. But, Mr. Traldi, it may create clarity and, therefore, if you would follow the suggestion raised by Mr. Lukic then, of course, it would perhaps assist the Chamber in getting the clarity on what is a matter still in dispute. Are you willing to follow that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am, and I'm also happy to have anyone else frame the question if they would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it's procedurally procedure where Mr. Lukic invited you to establish further clarity that you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It may take -- it may take me two or three questions since I don't have an exact sense of what he is looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Lukic wants this to be explored whether it was completed, yes or no. Further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're returning to the topic of Croats transported out of Central Bosnia in June of 1993. Now, first, is it your evidence that before the 12th and 13th of June, all the civilians who were being transported out of that area had already been transported out of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about dates here. I don't remember the dates, but I did take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, I think I'm unsure -- given the witness's inability to speak about dates, if there's any further clarification that Mr. Lukic would seek.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I would have to ask the witness to take off his earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you again take off your earphones. Mr. Lukic, any further suggestions for questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- what I would ask or I would ask you, Your Honour, to ask this witness, whether the transportation of civilians took more than seven days, and if the incarcerations, incarceration of HVO members and able-bodied men took more than 13 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll ask him --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he cannot talk about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps with some more open questions, I'll ask him whether he has any recollection of that. Could you please put on your earphones again. Witness, one more follow-up question on the civilians leaving in June 1993 and those who were in -- accommodated in Manjaca finally leaving. Even not knowing the dates, do you have any recollection as for how long they were in Manjaca before they left the Serb-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to be precise, but it was very soon after the civilians went out. It was seven to ten days maximum. I did not take part in the transportation of these people. Other colleagues took these people over, but they were there very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said: "Very soon after the civilians went out." What do you mean exactly by that, "the civilians went out"? Do you have a date for that, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the month of July 1993. But, really, I cannot remember the date. From Vlasic, we took them over and I know that there was a bus convoy that was organised, including, ambulances, and there were groups and we all had our different duties. Some went to Srbac-Davor where people crossed over to Croatia, then others as far as I know went somewhere towards Livno. I repeat and it's not first time I am saying this: I just took care of the wounded and sick people and they stayed in Banja Luka up to 15 days and then I drove them away as well that is the only thing can I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you are referring to the month of July 1993. We earlier looked at documents which were 8th of June, 10th of June, perhaps when they were processed. You are now talking about the month of July. Does that mean that it materialised only after some 20 days, or was it a mistake when you referred to July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said June. Well, maybe it was a permutation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm not familiar with the word "permutation." If someone could help me that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you again explain you said, "Well, maybe it was a" -- and could you then explain what you wanted to say? That is, about the confusion, June, July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it was summertime. I'm afraid, really, as far as these dates are concerned that I may make a mistake so if possible could be please not insist on these dates because I'm going make a mistake unintentionally and unconsciously. Throughout the war, I worked on exchanges every day and it is very hard for me to be precise with dates after all these years, even in terms of months but I know for sure that I took part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't insist on anything. You spontaneously mentioned July 1993 and that's why I asked the question. But you say I'm not certain about whether it was June or July. Mr. Lukic, I've tried to explore the matter. We leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have documents, Your Honour. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Of course, if the memory of witnesses is insufficiently to fully establish matters, then, of course, documentary evidence - as I said before - may assist us. No further questions? Mr. Krcmar, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, which is still a long way, and for having answered the many questions that were put to, both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could start with the next witness. We'd also could first take a break and the third option is that we give Mr. Tieger an opportunity to make a submission of his one-minute submission on the matter he announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In reviewing the transcript of Thursday's session we noticed an issue that might best be clarified at this time. Now the context was Mr. Lukic's reference to a shifting of the burden and the Trial Chamber's observations about the Defence taking time to correct matters that had not been presented as evidence to the Chamber. And as you'll recall at transcript page 32369, the Chamber addressed Mr. Lukic's remarks and the Court quite correctly and quite clearly stated that the Defence had no burden and that there had been no shift of the Prosecution's burden to the Defence. Then the following appears on the transcript: "The burden that the Defence bears is to rebut the Prosecution's case and that's all." So while the Chamber's position that the Defence has no burden was quite clear, out of an abundance of caution, we thought that we should bring this last passage to the Court's attention now for clarification, to ensure that the record reflects that it is the Prosecution's burden at all times to prove its cases beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Defence has no burden of proof at any time during the trial. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We take a break, and we'll resume ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I assumed that the Defence is ready to call its next witness, and the next witness will be examined by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sasa Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sasa Lukic. We're wondering when the first moment would be there. Welcome, Mr. Lukic, for the first time to examine the witness. MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your next witness would be Milivoje Simic. MR. S. LUKIC: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left, Mr. Sasa Lukic. And Mr. Lukic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. S. Lukic: MR. S. LUKIC: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Milivoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to the Ratko Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. MR. S. LUKIC: Can we have 65 ter 1D01685.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see the first page of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, this is my signature. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Can we also see the last page of the statement in B/C/S, i.e., in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has everything been accurately recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is everything truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Whatever I have stated is truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. S. LUKIC: Your Honour, I would like to tender the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D01685 receives number D921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D921 is admitted, absent any objections. Please proceed. MR. S. LUKIC: With your permission, I would like to read the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. MR. S. LUKIC: [Interpretation] Witness Milivoje Simic spent his entire career at the Doboj garrison. He remained there even after the conflict broke out in the territory of BiH. As a JNA officer, on the eve of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was engaged in Republic of Croatia, in Banja, from 15 September 1991 to 15 May 1992, i.e., up to the moment when the JNA surrendered its positions to UNPROFOR members. After leaving the territory of the Republic of Croatia, Witness Milivoje Simic withdrew to Doboj in Bosnia and Herzegovina together with his JNA unit. When the war started, he was the commander of the Doboj garrison. He witnessed artillery attacks on the town of Doboj even before the decision was made to establish the Army of Republika Srpska. He also witnessed attacks by Croatian forces on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
